why.core: The Learner Permit Test is a **reading** test as much as a driving one. It's full of technical words (*give way*, *merge*, *BAC*), rule words like **must**, **must not** and **may**, and diagrams you have to picture. Read carefully, and you'll pass. Then the rules you learn keep you, and your mates, alive.
why.extend: The Learner Permit Test assesses close reading: technical vocabulary, the precise force of modal verbs, conditional situations and diagrams. Reading strategically improves your score, and understanding the cause-and-effect reasoning behind each rule makes you a safer driver.

articles.title: How to get your Ls

body.support:
In Victoria, you can get your **learner permit** at **16**. First, you pass the **Learner Permit Test**. It has **32 questions**. You need **25 right** to pass.

**Read the handbook.** It's called *Road to Solo Driving*. Use the headings. Study the pictures.

**Learn the rule words.**

- **Must** = you **have to**.
- **Must not** = you're **not allowed**.
- **May** = you're **allowed**.

**Learn the signs.** A **yellow diamond** is a warning. A **red circle** tells you what you can't do.

**Test strategy.**

1. Read the **whole** question.
2. Find the **key words**.
3. **Picture** it.
4. Cross out wrong answers.

**On your Ls:** L plates front and back. A supervising driver. **Zero** alcohol. **No phone**, not even hands-free. Under 21? Log **120 hours**, with **20 at night**.
body.core:
In Victoria, you can get your **learner permit** at **16**. First, you pass the **Learner Permit Test**: **32 questions** on the road rules. You need **78%** (25 right). VicRoads has a free practice test.

**Read the handbook.** The questions come from the road rules in the official handbook, *Road to Solo Driving*. Don't read it like a novel. Use the headings to find a topic, read one section at a time, and study the diagrams.

**Learn the rule words.**

- **Must** means you **have to**. *You must give way to pedestrians.*
- **Must not** means you're **not allowed**. *You must not use a mobile phone.*
- **May** means you're **allowed**, but you don't have to.

Small words like *unless*, *except*, *always* and *never* can change the whole answer.

**Learn the sign language.** Signs speak in shapes and colours. A **red octagon** means stop. A **yellow diamond** warns you of something ahead. A **red circle** tells you what you can't do. A **green rectangle** gives directions.

**Use a test strategy.**

1. Read the **whole** question, slowly.
2. Find the **key words**: *must*, *turning right*, *unless*.
3. **Picture** the situation, or look closely at the diagram.
4. Read **every** option. Cross out the ones that are clearly wrong.
5. Choose the answer that matches the rule.

**Once you've got your Ls,** the rules are strict. You **must** display **L plates** on the front and back. You **must** have a **supervising driver** with a full licence. Your **BAC** must be **zero**. You **must not** use a phone at all, not even hands-free. And if you're under 21, you **must** log **120 hours** of supervised driving, including **20 at night**, before your P test.
body.extend:
In Victoria, you're eligible for a **learner permit** at **16**, after passing the **Learner Permit Test**: **32 questions** on the road rules, with a pass mark of **78%** (25 correct). VicRoads' free practice test is modelled on the real one.

**Read the handbook strategically.** Questions come from the official handbook, *Road to Solo Driving*. Use the headings to find topics. Read one section at a time. Treat diagrams as part of the text, because many questions depend on them.

**Read the modal verbs precisely.**

- **Must** creates an **obligation**: *You must give way to pedestrians.*
- **Must not** creates a **prohibition**: *You must not use a mobile phone.*
- **May** grants **permission**.

Conditional and absolute words (*unless*, *except*, *always*, *never*) often decide the answer.

**Read signs as a visual code.** Shape and colour signal function: a **red octagon** (stop), **yellow diamonds** (warnings), **red circles** (prohibitions) and **green rectangles** (direction).

**Use a test strategy.** Read the whole question. Find the key words. Picture the situation, or study the diagram. Cross out options that can't be right. Then choose the answer that matches the rule.

**On your Ls,** conditions are strict: **L plates** front and back, a **supervising driver** with a full licence, a **zero BAC**, and **no phone use at all**, including hands-free. Learners under 21 must also log **120 hours** of supervised driving, including **20 at night**, before the probationary licence test. Each rule exists because of a known risk, and understanding the cause makes it easier to follow.

caseStudies.title: Do the rules really work?

body.support:
In **2007**, Victoria made new rules for new drivers. It's why learners log 120 hours.

In **2017**, a study checked if the rules worked.

What it found:

- New P-platers were **19% less likely** to have a serious crash.
- New P-platers can only carry **one** passenger aged 16 to 22. Crashes with two or more young passengers dropped by **70%**.

But **speeding** and **phone** offences went **up**.

So the rules work, but only if drivers follow them.
body.core:
In **2007**, Victoria brought in tougher rules for new drivers, called the **Graduated Licensing System**. It's the reason learners under 21 have to log 120 hours of driving, and why new P-platers can't carry a car full of friends.

So, do the rules work? In **2017**, the government released an **evaluation**: a study that checked what had happened since the rules began.

Here's what it found:

- P-platers in their **first year** of driving were **19% less likely** to have a crash where someone was killed or seriously injured.
- The rule that limits new P-platers to **one passenger aged 16 to 22** made a big difference. Crashes while carrying **two or more** young passengers dropped by **70%**.

But it wasn't all good news. The study also found that **speeding** and **mobile phone** offences went **up** among P-platers.

So the rules save lives, but only when drivers follow them. Every rule in the handbook is there because of a real risk.
body.extend:
In **2007**, Victoria introduced a **Graduated Licensing System** (GLS) for new drivers. It includes the 120 hours of supervised driving for learners under 21. It also limits first-year P-platers to one passenger aged 16 to 22.

In **2017**, an **evaluation** of the system was released.

- First-year P-platers were **19% less likely** to be in a crash where someone was killed or seriously injured.
- After the **one-passenger** rule, crashes with two or more young passengers fell by **70%**.

The evaluation also found that **speeding** and **mobile phone** offences had **increased** among P-platers. It said more work was needed for older new drivers.

The evidence links specific rules to specific effects: fewer young passengers led to fewer crashes with young passengers. It also shows that a rule only reduces risk when people follow it.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** 32 questions; 25 correct (78%). Rules: L plates front and back, supervising driver, zero BAC, no phone, log hours. Strategy: read the whole question, find key words, picture it, cross out wrong answers.

**Sort:** L plates — must; phone — must not; night driving — may; supervising driver — must; any alcohol — must not; 120 hours — must.

**Signs:** red octagon — stop; upside-down triangle — give way; red circle with a line — something you must not do (e.g. no U-turn); green rectangle — directions; white rectangle with black writing — a regulatory rule (e.g. keep left).

**Road words (samples):** merge — join a lane smoothly; intersection — where roads meet or cross; overtake — pass another vehicle; supervising driver — a full-licence holder sitting with the learner; demerit points — penalty points for offences.

**Test question:** 1 situation; 2 key detail; 3 rule word (must); 4 correct answer (give way); 5 trap (indicating doesn't give right of way).

**Practice questions:** C (key words: may, phone); B (must, zero); B (red circle with a line = not allowed); B (under 21, 120, night).

**Case study:** first-year P-platers 19% less likely to have a fatal or serious crash; crashes with two or more peer passengers fell 70%; friends can distract, encourage risk-taking and add pressure; rules only work when followed.

realityCheck: **Not everyone will drive soon.** Cost, family circumstances or disability can make it a long way off. Frame the test as a close-reading challenge first.
**Rules change.** Check Transport Victoria and VicRoads pages before teaching; this course was written in 2026.
**Road trauma can be personal.** Some students have lost family or friends on the roads. Mention it before the case study, and keep it factual.
**Supervisors matter.** Students without a licensed adult at home may need help finding supervised hours. Some councils and community groups run L2P mentor programs.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students care about getting their Ls, and the practice test gives instant, honest feedback.
